extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; students of philosophy; general educated readers interested in human nature
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and interpretation of Michel de Montaigne's Essays (philosophical/reflective prose), focusing on arguments about human knowledge, imagination, custom, and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of reason and avoiding extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us therefore not look for certainty and stability. Our reason is always deceived by fickle shadows; nothing can fix the finite between the two Infinites, which both enclose and fly from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humans occupy a middle sphere and cannot perceive or grasp extremes; seeking absolute certainty or stability is misguided. Accept human epistemic limits rather than chasing absolute foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of knowing whole from part
rubrics_metrics.description: How can a part know the whole? ... the parts of the world are all so related and linked to one another, that I believe it impossible to know one without the other and without the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding any part (e.g., man) requires understanding its relations (place, time, motion, elements). Knowledge is holistic: parts and whole interdepend, making perfect knowledge of either impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing properties across categories (mind/body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all philosophers have confused ideas of things, and speak of material things in spiritual terms, and of spiritual things in material terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ascribe mental attributes (inclinations, fears) to lifeless bodies or spatial/motion attributes to minds; careful attention to category distinctions avoids conceptual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as deceptive and persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: It is that deceitful part in man, that mistress of error and falsity ... the more deceptive that she is not always so; for she would be an infallible rule of truth, if she were an infallible rule of falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination often overwhelms reason, convincing even the wisest; rhetoric, tone, and affect can persuade more than logical argument. Be wary of impressions that feel convincing but lack rational grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority through appearance and pageantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Our magistrates have known well this mystery. Their red robes, the ermine... were necessary; if the physicians had not their cassocks and their mules... they would never have duped the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremony, dress, and spectacle are used to command respect and substitute for substantive merit. Assess authority by substance, not by outward trappings (robes, guards, trumpets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom as second nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom makes men masons, soldiers, slaters... It is custom then which does this, for it constrains nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habits and upbringing shape beliefs, vocations, and 'natural' inclinations; what seems innate may be the product of repeated custom. Account for cultural/educational conditioning when evaluating dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty vs childhood impressions bias belief
rubrics_metrics.description: "Because you have believed from childhood that a box was empty when you saw nothing in it..." versus "Because you have been taught at school that there is no vacuum..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both novelty and early education can mislead; question whether beliefs arise from sensible perception, schooling, or mere habit. Avoid assuming childhood impressions or learned doctrines are intrinsically truer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and disease influence judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: We have another source of error in diseases. They spoil the judgment and the senses; and if the more serious produce a sensible change, I do not doubt that slighter ills produce a proportionate impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account a person's physical and mental state when evaluating their judgments; illness, mood, and bodily conditions can distort perception and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-love causes aversion to truth and self-deception
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of self-love... is to love self only and consider self only... This embarrassment... produces in him the most unrighteous and criminal passion... he conceives a mortal enmity against that truth which reproves him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect people (and yourself) to resist uncomfortable truths, hide faults, prefer flattery, and to shape appearances to be liked. Social interactions often involve concealment and mutual deceit; factor self-interest into judgments of testimony and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will influences belief by selecting aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: The will, which prefers one aspect to another, turns away the mind from considering the qualities of all that it does not like to see; and thus the mind... stops to consider the aspect which it likes, and so judges by what it sees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief is partly shaped by volition: what we want to be true biases what we attend to and accept. Recognize motivational influences when assessing beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid influencing others' judgments when soliciting opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: If we say, 'I think it beautiful,' 'I think it obscure,' ... we either entice the imagination into that view, or irritate it to the contrary. It is better to say nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asking for an honest appraisal, withhold your own evaluations to avoid biasing the other's judgment; silence often yields a purer, less contaminated response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education forms intuitions and may erase natural intuitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory, joy, are intuitions; and even mathematical propositions become intuitions, for education produces natural intuitions, and natural intuitions are erased by education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that training and schooling create 'instinctive' responses; what feels intuitive may be acquired. Be open to re-evaluating so-called natural intuitions in light of different education or experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inconstancy and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: We can never judge of the same thing exactly in the same way... I cannot judge of my work, while doing it. I must do as the artists, stand at a distance, but not too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that judgments fluctuate with perspective, mood, and time. Use distance and reflection to assess one's work, but acknowledge there is no perfectly stable judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination constructs reputation and value
rubrics_metrics.description: What but this faculty of imagination dispenses reputation, awards respect and veneration to persons, works, laws, and the great?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation and perceived value often derive from imaginative appraisal rather than intrinsic worth (e.g., approving a book by title). Scrutinize reputations and first impressions critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use knowledge of ruling passions to please or persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: By knowing each man's ruling passion, we are sure of pleasing him; and yet each has his fancies, opposed to his true good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding an individual's dominant drives or passions is a reliable means to gain favor or persuade, but those passions may not align with their true good—be ethically cautious in employing this tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pageantry compensates for lack of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: If magistrates had true justice, and if physicians had the true art of healing, they would have no occasion for square caps; the majesty of these sciences would of itself be venerable enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantive competence is lacking, institutions resort to symbols and ceremony to create authority. Evaluate institutional credibility by substantive capability rather than ceremonial signs.
